thread.title: Buy PEI: Even The Bears Are Giving It 32% Upside - Pennsylvania Real Estate Investment Trust (NYSE:PEI)

author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: Buy PEI: Even The Bears Are Giving It 32% Upside - Pennsylvania Real Estate Investment Trust (NYSE:PEI)
text:
Humans are scared to buy PREIT ( PEI ) because they see a stream of downgrades. JPMorgan recently downgraded PEI to “Underweight” while indicating 32.6% upside over the next year.
Since their buy ratings are unlikely to provide anywhere near a 32.6% return over the next year, this rating is fundamentally flawed. This demonstrates what academics have known for years: Wall Street ratings demonstrate exceptional correlation with past performance, but they have no correlation with future performance. However, Seeking Alpha articles and comments faired better .
Who would want to be caught with a neutral rating after shares tanked? They downgraded them after all the damage was done (share values already down over 40%).
However, the stream of downgrades could influence computers also if those computers are following news alerts.
We can see automated trading appears to have an incredible impact as well when we look at this historical price chart:
The chart starts on 9/11/2018, which is just before the preferred shares for CBL took their first hit of the fall season.
All 7 preferred shares from the “low quality” mall REITs, plus PEI and Washington Prime Group ( WPG ) declined between 33.4% and 40.1%. That is a remarkably tight range for 2 mall REITs common shares 7 mall REIT preferred shares. The only line to land outside the group was common shares from CBL Properties ( CBL ).
Correlation While common shares and preferred shares can demonstrate some correlation, the common and preferred shares should only cluster this tightly together when the preferred shares are convertible. These shares are much more "standard". Their value is driven by the expected stream of future dividend income.
Such synchronized dumping of shares is beyond what is normal for random chance. Preferred shares don’t trade efficiently enough to stay in such a tight pattern.
In The REIT Forum's weekly piece on preferred shares (subscription to The REIT Forum required), we provided ample examples of how preferred shares from the same REIT can move in different ways. We will include one example directly from that article here. It highlights the disconnect between two preferred shares from Chimera Investment Corporation ( CIM ). The shares are CIM-A ( CIM.PA ) and CIM-B ( CIM.PB ):
Sources: Schwab and The REIT Forum
While there are several preferred shares available from mortgage REITs at great prices, CIM-B is not one of them. Understanding that CIM-A and CIM-B disconnected very recently should convince investors that extremely correlation shouldn't be taken for granted.
The correlation demonstrated by the mall REITs and their preferred shares is exceptional.
Dividend Sustainability and Funds Available for Distribution PEI is getting some heat from analysts because they aren’t covering the dividend with FAD (Funds Available for Distribution). It’s like normalized FFO (Funds From Operations), but it strips out some recurring capital expenditures. Overall, it is a good measure with the exception of adding back stock-based compensation.
FAD is usually highest in Q4.
Analysts who were annualizing the first 3 quarters were getting a lower figure.
Over the trailing 12 month period FAD covered the dividend, though Q4 2018 should be a bit weaker due to some additional anchor replacement activities getting underway.
More of PEI's space will begin paying rent during 2019.
Consequently, it looks like the PEI won’t cover their dividend based on 2018 numbers .
The problem is that t his completely ignores the boost we should see in the second half of 2019. PEI has several anchor redevelopment projects coming online plus the grand opening of FDP (Fashion District of Philadelphia).
The projected FAD for 2020 , should be able to cover the common dividend with some room to spare. Management has been adamant about looking at their dividend sustainability in the long term, rather than cutting it when they have more projects under development.
Earnings Comparison Many investors who aren't primarily investing in equity REITs may not be familiar with terms like FFO and FAD. If you're familiar with other corporations, think of terms such as "Adjusted EPS" or "Normalized EPS". With FAD, we have a measure that is tracking cashflow much closer.
If Apple ( AAPL ) enters into contracts to sell a huge shipment of phones, they don't record the revenue until the phones are actually delivered. Even if AAPL gets paid today, they don't get to count it for "earnings" until they've delivered the goods .
Landlords have a similar situation. Even though they've already signed leases for some of this space, they don't get to recognize revenue until the tenant occupies the building. Because mall landlords often enter into leases well before the tenant moves in, we can have a little more clarity on their future revenues.
Preferred Shares It is worth noting that PEI should be looking to repurchase their preferred shares. It would be extremely accretive to earnings because of the extremely high yield. Since PEI doesn’t have any major maturities for the next few years, it shouldn’t cause balance sheet issues either.
With the common dividend set to be covered potentially in 2019 and much more effectively in 2020, the preferred shares should recover. They've been hammered over the last few months, which provides a compelling entry price.
It wouldn't be feasible for them to repurchase their entire outstanding amount, but they could put a dent in it.
Note: PEI's preferred shares are currently all between $15.00 and $16.00.
Conclusion Both PEI's common shares and their preferred shares went on sale. Their dividend doesn't look like it is covered in 2018, but growth in 2019 and 2020 should take care of that. It is critical to point out that we are NOT focused on growth generated from renewing leases at higher spreads. We are focused on growth coming from leases which are already signed. The opening of Fashion Districts of Philadelphia late in 2019 should create a significant boost to earnings in 2020.
At The REIT Forum, we believe it is critical to build analysis around the numbers for future periods. An emphasis on using past performance is causing analysts and computers to see REIT under intense pressure. As the REIT sold off low quality properties and invested in anchor redevelopment, it temporarily reduced revenue and earnings. Models built only on looking at current year earnings are missing the value from major developments.
The common market capitalization is around $400 million. Fashion Districts of Philadelphia cost around $200 million to build (for their half, around $400 million total). Ignoring the value of these developments that open next year leads to undervaluing the company and misunderstanding their dividend sustainability.
The REIT Forum focuses primarily on defensive investments with high growth potential. It is our objective to find quality investments at a discount, along with trading opportunities for the more active investors. Most of our research is on companies that are excellent investments over the long term.
Disclosure: I am/we are long PEI, PEI.PC, PEI.PD.
